title: Link v. Wabash Railroad Co.
lead: After six years of litigation over a train collision, William Link lost his negligence action when his lawyer missed a pretrial conference. The Supreme Court divided over whether that dismissal reflected permissible control of delay or unfair destruction of the client’s claim.

actors.name: Justice Harlan
actors.role: Author of the Supreme Court majority opinion

actors.name: Justice Black
actors.role: Dissenter joined by Chief Justice Warren

proceedings: A district court dismissed the action on its own initiative for failure to prosecute. The Seventh Circuit affirmed over a dissent, and the Supreme Court affirmed, 4–3, on June 25, 1962.
limits: No court decided the collision’s negligence merits. Justice Douglas dissented without a written opinion; Justices Frankfurter and White did not participate. The Court reserved dismissal for a single absence without other delay and the outcome of a supported Rule 60(b) reopening motion.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A collision claim survives an early defeat
paragraphs: William Link sought damages for injuries suffered when his vehicle collided with a Wabash Railroad Company train. He filed a diversity negligence action in August 1954. The district court initially entered judgment on the pleadings for the railroad, but the Seventh Circuit reversed in 1956. The Supreme Court denied the railroad's request for review in 1957, returning the case to the trial court.

A July 1957 trial setting was continued at Link's request without objection from the railroad. The district court later warned that it would dismiss the case unless it was retained. Link answered outstanding interrogatories the day before the show-cause hearing, more than nineteen months after service. The judge kept the case and set another trial. That setting was continued on the railroad's motion with Link's agreement. Additional interrogatories were answered in 1960 after an extension. The justices would disagree sharply about what this accumulated history demonstrated.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and prior proceedings, 627–629 n.2, 634–635 n.11

sections.title: The lawyer misses a conference
paragraphs: On September 29, 1960, the court notified both lawyers of a pretrial conference in Hammond, Indiana, scheduled for October 12 at 1 p.m. Link's lawyer told opposing counsel the preceding morning that he expected to attend. At approximately 10:45 on the conference morning, however, he called the judge's secretary from Indianapolis, about 160 miles away. He said he was preparing papers for the Indiana Supreme Court, was not actually arguing a case, and could come the next afternoon or on October 14 if the conference were reset.

Counsel did not appear at the appointed time. Two hours later the district court found his explanation unreasonable and dismissed Link's action on its own initiative for failure to prosecute, invoking its inherent authority. The Seventh Circuit affirmed over a dissent. Link obtained Supreme Court review of both the authority to act without a defendant's motion and the exercise of that authority here. The missed event was a pretrial conference, not the trial itself; the judicial account describes counsel's absence and attributes its consequences to Link.

sections.title: The rules leave a power to dismiss
sections.cue: The Supreme Court examines authority and notice
paragraphs: Justice Harlan wrote the Supreme Court's majority opinion. Link argued that Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b), which permits a defendant to seek dismissal for failure to prosecute, made a defendant's motion necessary. The Court rejected that negative implication. The rule did not clearly remove the longstanding judicial power to prevent undue delay and manage proceedings, including dismissal with prejudice on the court's initiative. Historical nonsuit practice, decisions recognizing inherent authority, and local practices for clearing stale cases supported that conclusion. The opinion's survey of local rules did not mean that one particular listed rule governed this dismissal. Rule 83 also permitted consistent regulation of matters the rules did not specifically address.

Lack of advance notice of dismissal or a preliminary adversary hearing did not automatically invalidate this order. Due process required a meaningful opportunity to be heard, but the adequacy of procedure depended partly on what the circumstances communicated about the consequences of the conduct. In this record the majority found another warning and hearing unnecessary. It did not announce that calling a sanction inherent dispenses with notice in every case.

sources.pinpoint: Inherent authority and procedural protections, 629–633 nn.3–8

sections.title: The entire history sustains this dismissal
sections.cue: Discretion, reopening, and responsibility for counsel
paragraphs: The majority considered the telephone explanation inadequate and thought counsel's absence, combined with the preceding delays, permitted an inference of deliberate delay. This was the oldest civil matter on the district court's docket. Link's initial post-remand continuance, the overdue interrogatories, agreement to a later continuance, and lack of affirmative efforts to reach trial answered the contention that all delay belonged to the railroad or the court.

The Court expressly left open whether an unexplained absence from a pretrial conference, standing alone with no other dilatoriness, justified dismissal with prejudice. Even if the appellate opinion could be read more broadly, the supported district-court ground allowed a narrower affirmance. Counsel had notice of the conference; the record did not establish inability to attend beyond his control.

The availability of relief from judgment under Rule 60(b) also reduced the majority's concern about omitted advance procedures. Link never asked the district court to reopen the judgment with a better explanation. The Court did not decide whether denying a supported motion of that kind would have abused discretion.

Finally, the majority attributed the acts and omissions of Link's voluntarily chosen lawyer to Link under ordinary representative litigation. Requiring the railroad to continue defending merely to spare Link those consequences would shift their burden to the defendant. Malpractice litigation might provide a remedy for substantially deficient representation, but the Court neither found malpractice nor awarded anything against the attorney.

sections.title: Black rejects the loss of the client’s claim
sections.cue: The written dissent and the judgment
paragraphs: Justice Black, joined by Chief Justice Warren, read the case differently. In his view, the lower courts had punished the missed conference rather than established general non-prosecution. Much of the case's age followed the railroad's erroneous pleading victory and ensuing review. Other delays involved agreed continuances or ongoing litigation. The district court had already retained the case after a show-cause hearing, and counsel's request to reschedule itself indicated continued prosecution.

Black accepted that courts could discipline lawyers and that clients sometimes bear their decisions' consequences. He opposed mechanically extending those propositions to extinguishing an innocent client's valuable cause of action without warning. An ordinary client could reasonably rely on a licensed lawyer instead of monitoring every procedural task. Black distinguished the majority's criminal-waiver authorities and rejected the availability of Rule 60(b) as an adequate response to the client's lack of notice. He also doubted the efficiency rationale: dismissing potentially meritorious claims could generate years of appeals, as this litigation illustrated.

Justice Douglas separately dissented without a written explanation. Justices Frankfurter and White did not participate. On June 25, 1962, the Court affirmed by a 4–3 vote, leaving the negligence action dismissed without a trial on the collision. The reserved single-absence question and the unfiled reopening motion remained unresolved.

sources.pinpoint: Black dissent, 636–649 and dissent nn.1–13; disposition, 635–636
